title: How to Address Imbalanced Datasets?
description: Random undersampling and oversampling, SMOTE, algorithm choice, and loss penalties for classification problems with skewed classes.
content:
In many real-world **classification** problems, the classes are far from evenly represented - for example, fraudulent transactions make up only a tiny fraction of all transactions. Such **imbalanced datasets** require special treatment, because a model that simply predicts the majority class can look accurate while being practically useless.

There are quite a few ways to handle imbalanced datasets:
• Random undersampling
• Random oversampling
• Synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE)
• Choosing learning algorithms wisely
• Penalizing minority-class mistakes in the loss function

**Random undersampling** randomly eliminates samples from the majority class until the classes are balanced in the remaining dataset. This approach is generally used when the dataset has a huge amount of training data. However, random elimination can erase some useful knowledge from the training dataset.

**Random oversampling** takes the opposite approach: instead of eliminating, it replicates the instances of the minority class until the classes are balanced. An important thing to remember: the train-test split should be applied before the oversampling technique in order to avoid confusion in evaluation.

**Synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE)** is a cleverer approach: a subset of the minority class is taken and synthetic data is generated based on it (typically by interpolating between existing minority samples and their nearest neighbors). These synthetic data points are then added to the original dataset as additional examples of the minority class - so instead of copying the same samples over and over, the model sees slightly new variations of the minority class.

It is also a good practice to choose learning algorithms wisely: decision tree-based algorithms can handle imbalanced datasets well, and boosting and bagging techniques are also good choices for imbalanced datasets.

Finally, one can put an additional penalty on the loss function every time the model misclassifies the minority class. This forces the model to pay more attention to the minority class and try to make fewer mistakes on it.
